name: The Brouwer Fixed-Point Theorem
statement: Any continuous way of stirring a disc back into itself must leave at least one point exactly where it started.
statementAccent: must leave at least one point exactly where it started
meaning: The Brouwer fixed-point theorem states that any continuous function from a closed ball to itself has at least one fixed point, a point that the function leaves unmoved. In the plane this means any continuous deformation of a disc into itself pins at least one point in place; the same holds for a solid ball in any dimension, and more generally for any convex compact set. Vividly, if you stir a cup of coffee continuously and let it settle, some molecule ends up exactly where it began, and a crumpled map of a country laid flat on itself has one point lying over its true location. It is a landmark of topology, remarkable for guaranteeing a fixed point without any hint of where it is.
mechanism: The theorem is topological, resting on the fact that a solid ball cannot be continuously retracted onto its boundary sphere without tearing. Suppose a continuous self-map had no fixed point; then every point and its image would differ, and one could draw a ray from the image through the point to the boundary, defining a continuous retraction of the ball onto its edge. But no such retraction exists, a fact detected by algebraic invariants like the degree of a map or homology groups that distinguish the ball from its boundary. The contradiction forces a fixed point. In one dimension the theorem reduces to the intermediate value theorem applied to the function minus the identity, which must cross zero.

examples.text: Stir a cup of coffee and let it come to rest; the theorem guarantees at least one point of the fluid returns to exactly where it started before stirring.
Lay a map of a region flat on top of that very region; some point on the map lies directly above the actual place it represents, however you crumple it.
John Nash used a fixed-point argument, via Kakutani's generalisation of Brouwer's theorem, to prove that every finite game has an equilibrium, a foundation of game theory.

variants.name: Kakutani's theorem
variants.text: A generalisation to set-valued maps, guaranteeing a fixed point for suitable correspondences, the form used to prove the existence of Nash and market equilibria in economics.

variants.name: The Schauder extension
variants.text: The Schauder fixed-point theorem carries the result to infinite-dimensional spaces, a key tool for proving that differential and integral equations have solutions.

whyItMatters: The Brouwer fixed-point theorem is a cornerstone of topology and one of the most widely applied existence results in mathematics. Through Kakutani's and Schauder's generalisations it proves the existence of Nash equilibria in game theory, competitive equilibria in economics, and solutions to differential and integral equations across analysis. It is also a philosophically striking result, guaranteeing that a fixed point must exist while giving no way to find it, a purely non-constructive certainty. And it drove the development of algebraic topology, since the tools invented to prove it, degree theory and homology, became central instruments of modern geometry.

working.text: when a continuous process maps a convex compact set into itself, invoke the theorem to assert a fixed point, an equilibrium, exists.
prove it by contradiction: a fixed-point-free self-map would yield an impossible continuous retraction of the ball onto its boundary.
use Kakutani for set-valued maps in economics and Schauder for infinite-dimensional spaces in the theory of differential equations.

limits: The theorem requires the domain to be a compact convex set, or a space topologically equivalent to a ball; it fails for shapes with holes, like an annulus or a circle, where a rotation moves every point. It fails for unbounded or open regions, since a translation on the whole plane has no fixed point, and it fails without continuity. Above all it is non-constructive: it certifies that a fixed point exists but supplies no procedure to locate it, and there may be many, so it answers whether but never where, a limitation that motivated later constructive and computational fixed-point methods.
misreadings: The theorem guarantees existence, not uniqueness or location; there may be one fixed point or many, and it never says where they are. It applies to continuous maps of a ball or convex compact set into itself, not to spaces with holes, so a rotation of a ring, which fixes nothing, is no counterexample because the ring is not a disc. And its famous non-constructivity is genuine: the standard proofs, ironically given Brouwer's own intuitionist philosophy, establish a fixed point exists without any means of exhibiting it.
origin: Proved in the general n-dimensional case by L.E.J. Brouwer in 1911, with the three-dimensional case shown earlier by Piers Bohl in 1904; later generalised by Kakutani to set-valued maps and by Schauder to infinite-dimensional spaces.
